concept: TestFlight designated requirement and Gatekeeper launch of a store-signed Mac build
summary: Source-anchored research for TestFlight designated requirement and Gatekeeper launch of a store-signed Mac build. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Apple TN3127 documents codesign --display -r - <app> as a way to inspect an app’s designated requirement. Inspect the exact App Store Connect or TestFlight app under investigation because a development-signed variant can carry a different requirement from the store-distributed variant. (high confidence)

Apple’s notarization documentation says software distributed through the Mac App Store does not require separate notarization because App Store submission includes equivalent security checks. The electron-builder Mac App Store guide reports the same split between store distribution and direct Developer ID distribution. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-29)

The original Mac App Store distribution-signed archive is not a supported general-purpose local launch artifact. Apple says macOS may sometimes run it, but this is unsupported and can fail when the app claims restricted entitlements. Apple identifies TestFlight as a pre-release testing route because it re-signs the app. This separates uploading the archive from running the TestFlight-installed copy. (medium confidence)

A designated requirement (DR) is the code identity test embedded in a signature, and macOS can use it to recognize the same code during later authorization checks. Apple documents `codesign -d -r- <app>` as a way to display the DR. Apple also says TestFlight re-signs an app for testing; therefore, inspect the installed TestFlight artifact itself rather than treating the pre-upload archive's DR as conclusive (the last sentence is an inference from Apple's re-signing description). (medium confidence)

Apple TN3127 says an Apple Development designated requirement differs from the requirements used by Developer ID and Mac App Store apps; it explicitly says a Mac App Store app will not satisfy the Apple Development requirement, or vice versa. Apple’s code requirements guide says codesign typically derives a default designated requirement from the program name and signature chain when the signer supplies no explicit requirement. (high confidence)

Apple's current Xcode guide groups TestFlight and App Store delivery under App Store Connect and says that channel uses an Apple Developer Program distribution provisioning profile. Apple also says TestFlight re-signs the app much like the App Store. Do not treat the local pre-upload Apple Distribution identity as a complete description of the delivered TestFlight artifact. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-29)

A sample `spctl --list` output in the PyOxidizer Apple code-signing guide labels a `[Testflight]` rule `allow execute` and lists separate `[Mac App Store]` rules for `allow install` and `allow execute`. This is sample policy output, not a guarantee that current macOS releases use the same labels or requirements. (low confidence)

Apple’s DTS Gatekeeper troubleshooting guidance focuses on Developer ID-signed code and recommends strict codesign verification; it says Gatekeeper should not block App Store apps. A separate third-party release audit says its signature, notarization, and stapling checks did not install the package. Implementation inference for TestFlight: inspect the delivered beta’s signature and designated requirement and test its actual launch separately, without assuming Developer ID Gatekeeper guidance applies unchanged. (medium confidence)

A 2024 electron-builder issue reports that an app installed through TestFlight failed to launch. The author said a Developer ID installer package passed notarization but failed Transporter validation, while a Mac App Store installer package passed Transporter but failed notarization. The author later reported success after enabling electron-builder’s notarization option and expressed a belief that it notarized the app before packaging. This is one self-reported workflow result and does not establish that all TestFlight builds require notarization. (low confidence)

Xcode documents App Store Connect as the distribution method for apps delivered through TestFlight or the App Store, signed with an Apple Developer Program distribution provisioning profile. The electron-builder Mac App Store guide identifies Mac App Distribution as the app signing certificate and Mac Installer Distribution as the uploaded package certificate. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-22)

Apple’s Xcode launch simulation uses spctl -a -v and quarantined copies for Developer ID-signed apps. Mac Hardening’s September 2026 guide says Mac App Store apps report their own spctl source and that a rejected result predicts rejection if the app were quarantined. Do not treat a Developer ID notarization result as the expected Gatekeeper label for a TestFlight build. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-22)

In electron-builder issue 8382, the author reported that a Developer ID installer package passed notarization but failed Transporter checks, while a Mac App Store installer package passed Transporter but failed notarization. The author later reported resolving the case by enabling electron-builder’s notarization option and said they believed it notarized the app before packaging. This self-report illustrates separate validation outcomes; it does not establish that a TestFlight build needs Developer ID notarization. (medium confidence)
